# Nehemiah 8 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records a pivotal moment: the public reading of the Law by Ezra, the people’s response of weeping followed by joy, and the rediscovery and celebration of the Feast of Tabernacles (Booths). Dr. Constable notes the threefold structure: “intellectual response to the Word (vv. 1–8), emotional response to the Word (vv. 9–12), and volitional response to the Word (vv. 13–18).”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-8.html

Derek Kidner writes, “This day was to prove a turning-point. From now on, the Jews would be predominantly ‘a people of the book.’”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-8-commentary

---

## v. 1 — The People Gather and Request the Law

**“All the people gathered together as one man in the square before the Water Gate.”** Gill notes the square was a large, commodious street leading to the Water Gate (cf. Neh. 3:26). The phrase “as one man” is a Hebrew idiom expressing great unanimity, zeal, and affection. The Water Gate was on the east side of the new city wall, just south of Ophel, near the Gihon Spring. It was the place of justice and social life in ancient Jewish communities.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-8-commentary

**“They asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses.”** This was the people’s initiative—they demanded the reading; Ezra did not have to urge them. Gill suggests Ezra had come to Jerusalem thirteen years earlier (Ezra 7:6) but had likely returned to Babylon and only recently come back. “The Book of the Law of Moses” refers to the Pentateuch (Genesis–Deuteronomy) and possibly all Scripture received by that time; Ezra is generally believed to have been largely responsible for organizing the OT canon.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-8-commentary

**Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** The people’s desire to gather and hear God’s word is itself evidence that the Spirit of God was already at work in them *before* the reading even begins. “People do not gather together as one man for the things of God unless the Spirit of God has moved them.” J. Edwin Orr’s definition of revival — “The Spirit of God working through the Word of God, in the lives of the people of God” — is exemplified in this chapter.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

**Matthew Henry:** Sacrifices were to be offered only at the temple door, but praying and preaching were services of religion as acceptably performed in one place as another. Masters of families should bring their families with them to public worship. Women and children have souls to save and must acquaint themselves with God’s word.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-8-commentary

---

## v. 2 — The Timing and the Congregation

**“On the first day of the seventh month.”** Gill explains this was the month Tishri (September/October), and this specific day was a triple holy day: (1) the first of every month was a festival, (2) the first of the seventh month was the Feast of Trumpets (Lev. 23:24), and (3) it was New Year’s Day of the civil year. Jarchi confirms this was the first day of the year. It was also the day the altar was first set up after the return from captivity (Ezra 3:6).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

**“Men and women and all who could listen and understand.”** This included adults of both sexes (Gill notes Grotius thought women had a separate place) and all under-age children who were capable of hearing the law read to some advantage.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

---

## v. 3 — Six Hours of Reading

**“Ezra read it aloud from daybreak until noon.”** That is about six hours. Enduring Word notes “from morning” is literally “from the light” — these people gathered from dawn, willing to sacrifice to hear God’s word. Gill says Ezra read selected passages here and there, not the whole Pentateuch in order, and was likely relieved at times by the men with him.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

**“All the people listened attentively.”** Gill cites Maimonides, who gathered from this that as soon as the reader begins reading the law, it is not lawful to speak about anything — not even the constitutions of the law — but only to attend silently.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

---

## v. 4 — The Wooden Platform and the Thirteen Assistants

**“Ezra the scribe stood on a high wooden platform built for this occasion.”** Gill notes the Hebrew text calls this a “tower” (Latin: *turris ligni*), partly because of its height, partly because of its form, and partly for its largeness — it held fourteen men. The pulpit was made so Ezra could be plainly seen and more easily heard. Aben Ezra observes that the pulpits in later Jewish synagogues were made after the same pattern and called by the same name.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

**The thirteen men:** Six at his right (Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, Maaseiah) and seven at his left (Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hash-baddanah, Zechariah, Meshullam). Gill says they stood there not merely in honour to Ezra and as approvers of the truth of what he read, but to relieve him when he grew weary.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

Enduring Word adds that the ministry of God’s word has the greatest effect when people can see men who support it and are in obedience to it.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

---

## v. 5 — The People Stand in Reverence

**“As he opened it, all the people stood up.”** They stood to hear better and in honour and reverence of the law. Gill records that the Jews had a tradition: from the times of Moses to Rabban Gamaliel, they learned the law only standing; after his death a disease came into the world, and they learned it sitting. By later rabbinic canon, it is not necessary to stand at the reading of the law.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

Enduring Word: “They recognized it for what it was — the word of God, not the word of man. They honored it.” This is evidence both that the Spirit of God is at work and that something good is going to happen.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

---

## v. 6 — Ezra’s Blessing and the People’s Response

**“Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God.”** Before he began to read, Ezra addressed God in a short prayer of benediction — ascribing blessing, honour, and glory to him, celebrating his being and perfections. Gill notes that Maimonides records this became synagogue custom: the reader, after opening the book, says, “Blessed art thou, O Lord our God, King of the world, who hath chosen us out of all people, and hath given us his law,” and all the people answer “Amen.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

**“Amen, Amen!”** The doubling expressed hearty assent. The Jews had many rules about pronouncing the “Amen” — that it must not be too quick, curt, or short, nor with too high a voice.

**“With their hands uplifted … they bowed down and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.”** Lifting up hands was a prayer gesture (cf. 1 Tim. 2:8). Constable notes that lifting hands toward heaven, normally with palms upward, was a common way Jews expressed their desire to receive a blessing from God. Bowing with faces to the ground reflected humility before God — the posture of slaves before their masters in the ancient world.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-8.html

Enduring Word sees three immediate results of the word-and-Spirit work: (1) thanksgiving (Amen), (2) prayer (uplifted hands), (3) worship (bowing down).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

---

## vv. 7–8 — The Levites Explain the Law

**v. 7 — Thirteen Levites “instructed the people in the Law as they stood in their places.”** Gill says these Levites (Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, etc.) also “caused the people to understand the law” alongside Ezra. The people stayed in their place from morning to noon — both attentive and constant. It is plain Ezra did not only read but also gave the sense, especially where there was difficulty.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

**v. 8 — “They read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight.”** This verse is crucial and much discussed:

- **Gill:** “They read distinctly” means clear and distinct pronunciation. Gill doubts the translation-into-Chaldee theory (that Hebrew was rendered into Aramaic for those used to the Chaldee language in Babylon). He thinks it describes clear enunciation first, then explanation. The Talmudists understood “distinctly” as the Targum (Chaldee translation), “the sense” as the verses or accents, and “the reading” as the distinction of accents.
- **Ellicott:** “Gave the sense” — they expounded obscurer passages, and in doing so naturally translated into the vernacular Aramaic dialect. “Caused them to understand the reading” simply explains the former: they expounded as they read.
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** They read, explained, and gave the sense, and the hearers attended to/understood the reading. It was paraphrastic exposition and application of the law — not a distinct recitation according to appointed rules.
- **Pulpit Commentary:** They read distinctly so every word could be heard. They translated Hebrew into the popular Aramaic/Chaldee and explained the meaning of each passage.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/nehemiah/8.htm

**Precept Austin / Steven Cole:** The teachers made the reading of Scripture clear and gave the meaning. Probably Ezra would read a section and then his assistants, perhaps in smaller groups, would expound to make the meaning clear. “For spiritual renewal, God’s Word must be taught.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-8-commentary

**Constable:** “Ezra and his associates not only translated the Law, they also explained what it meant and how it applied to the people. This is true Bible exposition.” The ceremony reflects the form of Israelite worship that had developed in exile — almost the same elements that characterised synagogue services: assembly, request for Torah reading, opening the scroll, standing, praise, response, instruction (sermon), oral explanation, and fellowship meal.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-8.html

**John Piper (Desiring God / Reformed Baptist):** Calls this “the beginning of the synagogue form that you bump into in the New Testament.” Ezra and the Levites “read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading.”
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pastor-as-prophet-session-2

**Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** Understanding must be the preacher’s first goal. “If people leave knowing five helpful hints to a better life, but do not have a greater understanding of God’s word, the preacher has failed.” The preacher must communicate the sense of the passage, not his own agenda.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

---

## v. 9 — The People Weep

**“This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep.”** Nehemiah the governor, Ezra, and the Levites all spoke this. The day was holy because it was both the new moon and the Feast of Trumpets. Mourning was unsuitable to a festival where trumpets were to be blown and gladness shown (Num. 10:10).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

**“For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law.”** Gill explains they wept because they perceived they had not kept the law but had broken it in many instances, and were therefore liable to the wrath and judgment of God in case of disobedience.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

Constable adds: “Conviction of their departure from God’s will fell on the people as they heard the Law read. Their initial reaction was to mourn and weep.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-8.html

Enduring Word: “The word of God was doing its intended work. 2 Timothy 3:16 tells us two things that the word of God is profitable for: reproof and correction. Sometimes it hurts to be reproved and corrected, and these tears were evidence of some of that pain.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

---

## v. 10 — “The Joy of the LORD Is Your Strength”

**“Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared.”** Gill: “Eat the fat” means the richest provisions, the best food and drink — not a common meal but a feast. Sending portions to those who had nothing was for the poor (the widow, fatherless, and stranger), who at festivals were to partake of the entertainment (Deut. 16:11).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

**“Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”** This is the most quoted verse of the chapter. A significant exegetical debate surrounds the word translated “strength.”

### The “Strength” vs. “Stronghold” Debate

**John Piper (Desiring God / Reformed Baptist)** offers an extended treatment. The Hebrew word is ***ma‘ōz*** (מָעוֹז), used 37 times in the Hebrew OT. In the ESV it is translated 14 times as “stronghold,” 7 times as “refuge,” 7 times as “fortress,” 3 times as “protection” — and only *once* as “strength,” namely here in Nehemiah 8:10. Piper says, “I am totally baffled as to why that is.” He argues that the context confirms “stronghold”: the people are weeping in grief over their sin and guilt (elaborated in Nehemiah 9:33, “we have acted wickedly”). The answer of the verse is: “There’s a refuge! There’s a stronghold. There’s a fortress. There’s a protection against what grieves you — your sin and God’s holy judgment. And what is that protection, that stronghold? It is your joy in the Lord. … Joy in God your Savior is your refuge.”

Piper also argues that “the joy of the LORD” here means *our joy in the Lord*, not *the Lord’s joy over us* (though the latter is a glorious biblical truth — e.g., Zeph. 3:17). The three parallel statements in vv. 9–12 all point to the *rejoicing that replaces grieving*.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-joy-of-the-lord-is-your-stronghold

**Gill** (traditional reading): “The joy of the Lord is your strength” — to rejoice as the Lord commanded on such days was a means of increasing both bodily strength and inward strength. The joy which has the Lord for its object, and comes from him, is the cause of renewing spiritual strength, so as to run and not be weary, walk and not faint. Gill understands “joy of the Lord” as both the joy God gives and the joy directed toward God.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

**Enduring Word:** Even when convicted of sin, “we can be glad because God is doing a great work. … Our knowledge of our sin should never be bigger than our knowledge of Jesus as our Savior.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

**Ligonier (Reformed):** “One of the strengths of Reformed theology is that it has a solid biblical understanding of total depravity. … But we must not focus only on our sin and our depravity; instead, we must focus on what Christ has done for us. … Nehemiah 8:10 is right when it says, ‘And do not be grieved, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.’”
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joy-and-strength

**Constable:** “This joy, as they thought about Yahweh, would strengthen and sustain them as a tonic.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-8.html

---

## v. 11 — The Levites Calm the People

**“Be still, since today is holy. Do not grieve.”** Gill says the Levites made the people quiet and easy, backed by the governor. They were to refrain from weeping and mourning outwardly, and not to cherish grief inwardly — because the day was a festival, set apart for joy and gladness.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

---

## v. 12 — The People Rejoice

**“All the people began to eat and drink, to send out portions, and to rejoice greatly, because they understood the words that had been made known to them.”** Gill: They made great mirth, with music (vocal and instrumental), because they had understood the words — the meaning of the several laws read and explained. He adds: “How much more reason is there for joy and gladness, when the Gospel, and the doctrines of it, are clearly known and understood? (Psalm 89:15).”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

Piper notes the progression: in v. 8 they had understood something correctly but not everything — they wept. In v. 12 “they stopped weeping and rejoiced ‘because they understood what was declared to them.’ … The light was dawning that you can’t honor Yahweh as holy if you only grieve in his presence. Grief is good. Fear is good. Penitence is good. Tears are good. But not if that’s all you feel. God’s holiness is the purity and perfection not only of his justice but also of his mercy and grace. And cowering people do not magnify the glory of grace.”
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-joy-of-the-lord-is-your-stronghold

---

## v. 13 — The Leaders Return for Deeper Study

**“On the second day of the month, the heads of all the families, along with the priests and Levites, gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law.”** Gill notes that even priests and Levites, though instructors of others, needed to be taught themselves — “which was highly commendable in them.” They came to Ezra for better information on difficult points they had observed the day before, and to be better equipped to teach the people.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

Enduring Word: “Leaders have a special need to understand and walk in God’s word. Their ignorance or disobedience affects far more than themselves.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

Constable: “Note that the spiritually revived people had an insatiable appetite to learn more about God’s Word. This is a normal outcome of true revival.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-8.html

---

## vv. 14–15 — Rediscovering the Feast of Tabernacles

**v. 14 — “They found written in the Law … that the Israelites were to dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month.”** Gill says this was found either by hearing it read the day before or by conversation with Ezra. The specific reference is Leviticus 23:39ff. The feast was to begin on the fifteenth of the month — only two weeks away.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

**v. 15 — The proclamation about branches.** Gill clarifies that Ezra and those with him gave orders for heralds to proclaim in all cities that the Feast of Tabernacles would be kept. This proclamation was not commanded in the Law itself; it was their own practical order. The branches (olive, wild olive/pine, myrtle, palm, and leafy trees) were to be fetched from the Mount of Olives and other mountains around Jerusalem. Gill notes the branches were not for making the booths themselves (which were made of boards and planks) but for decorating them. Aben Ezra interprets the list disjunctively — any sort of branch would do, not all of them.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

---

## vv. 16–17 — The People Build and Dwell in Booths

**v. 16 — Booths everywhere.** “On their own rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, and in the squares by the Water Gate and by the Gate of Ephraim.” Roofs in that culture were flat (Deut. 22:8). The booths could be made anywhere, so long as they were open to the air. The priests and Levites made theirs in the temple courts. None were erected outside the city walls for fear of enemies.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

Constable notes that the Feast of Tabernacles had special significance for the returned exiles: it looked back to Israel’s wilderness wanderings *and* forward to permanent residence in the Promised Land. The returnees themselves had “come through a kind of wilderness experience” and “even had to travel through a literal wilderness to get back to their land.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-8.html

**v. 17 — “From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this.”** This statement has prompted much discussion:

- **Gill:** The feast had been observed since Joshua (1 Kings 8:2; Ezra 3:4 prove it), but *not so* — not with such exactness, such zeal and affection, such a regard to the law of God as to read it every day of the feast, and with such joy and gladness. Gill explicitly rejects the theory of a textual corruption (one scholar had proposed “Joshua” should be “Josiah”). The “very great gladness” came because they were restored to their land, had the book of the law and knowledge of it, and were enabled to observe it.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

- **Constable:** The restoration community had observed the Feast of Tabernacles previously (Ezra 3:4); however, the present celebration was the most festive and well-attended one since Joshua had brought the Israelites into the Promised Land. This reflects “growing joy and spiritual strength among the Jews who returned from exile.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-8.html

- **Enduring Word:** “Their attitude was that God said it, so we will do it. Even though tradition did not tell them to keep the Feast of Tabernacles … they relied on God’s word, not on tradition.” The Feast was about remembering God’s provision in the wilderness; they could see God’s blessing and provision for them right then, and “it made something old seem brand new to them.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

---

## v. 18 — Seven Days of Reading, Eighth-Day Assembly

**“Day after day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God.”** Gill notes that Ezra read every day during the feast, whereas only the first and last days were the holy convocations on which the law seems normally to have been read. The feast was kept seven days, and “on the eighth day was a solemn assembly, according to the manner” (prescribed in Lev. 23:39).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm

Enduring Word: “This revival began by the Spirit of God working through the word of God; it continued that way also.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### “Strength” vs. “Stronghold” (v. 10)

- **John Piper / Desiring God (Reformed Baptist):** Insists the Hebrew *ma‘ōz* should be translated “stronghold,” “refuge,” or “fortress,” not “strength,” and that the “joy of the Lord” means *our* joy in God, which becomes a place of refuge from sin and guilt. He critiques virtually all modern English translations on this point.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-joy-of-the-lord-is-your-stronghold

- **Traditional Evangelical / Pentecostal (Enduring Word, Gill, most translations):** Retain “strength” and understand the joy of the Lord as a source of spiritual and even physical strengthening, enabling believers to serve God with cheerfulness. Enduring Word connects it to knowing Jesus as a greater Savior than we are sinners.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

### Revival Emphasis (Pentecostal/Charismatic vs. Reformed)

- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** The chapter is read through the lens of revival — the Spirit’s work is highlighted repeatedly. “People who will be attentive to the Book of the Law for some six hours are people touched by the Spirit of God.” The chapter is presented as a paradigm of cooperating with the Spirit’s work.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-8/

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** Connects the passage to the balance between total depravity and gospel joy. “We need to talk about our sin and we need to repent … But we must not focus only on our sin and our depravity.” The chapter is read more as a lesson in the proper proportion of grief and joy in the Christian life.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joy-and-strength

- **Desiring God (Reformed Baptist):** The chapter is handled with careful exegetical rigour (the *ma‘ōz* point), yet also draws the strong conclusion that “the fear of God, without joy in God, is no refuge from the wrath of God” — very much in the “Christian Hedonism” framework Piper is known for.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-joy-of-the-lord-is-your-stronghold

### The Nature of the “Reading and Explaining” (vv. 7–8)

- **Older commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Keil & Delitzsch, Pulpit):** Debate whether the Levites translated Hebrew into Aramaic (Chaldee) for the people or simply explained obscurities. Gill leans toward explanation without translation; Ellicott and Pulpit see translation as naturally part of the process, given the people’s long exposure to Aramaic in Babylon.
- **Modern evangelical (Constable, Cole/Precept Austin):** See the passage as a model of true expository preaching — reading Scripture, then giving the sense and application. Constable explicitly calls it “true Bible exposition.”
- **Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Sees this as the historical beginning of the synagogue form of worship that appears in the NT.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pastor-as-prophet-session-2

---

## Catholic and Orthodox Readings

I was unable to fetch specific Catholic or Orthodox commentaries on Nehemiah 8 within the search and fetch limits. The approved Catholic site (newadvent.org, catholic.com) and Orthodox site (oca.org) would be the appropriate places to consult for those traditions’ readings, particularly regarding the liturgical significance of the public reading of Scripture and whether this passage informs the Church’s understanding of the Liturgy of the Word.

---

## Modern Scholarship

I was unable to fetch pages from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the limits, but Constable (an evangelical scholar) references the view that the ceremony in Nehemiah 8 “reflects the form of Israelite worship that had developed in exile” and was the prototype of later synagogue services — a view shared by critical scholars like Williamson.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-8.html

The Precept Austin notes cite Bob Utley rejecting “modern JEDP source criticism” (the documentary hypothesis that the Pentateuch was pieced together by later redactors) and holding to Mosaic authorship, though acknowledging that someone like Ezra or Jeremiah may have done final editing.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-8-commentary

---

## Debated Popular Modern Teaching

No results were returned concerning prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace readings of Nehemiah 8. The “joy of the Lord is your strength” verse (v. 10) is frequently cited in popular devotion and contemporary worship music, and could potentially be co-opted by prosperity teaching to suggest that joy unlocks divine strength for earthly success. However, I found no page within the approved sites that documents such an interpretation; the traditional and Reformed sources all treat the verse in terms of spiritual refuge, gospel joy, and covenant renewal.
